title: Eruption types and volcano shape
keyIdea: Volcanoes do not all erupt the same way. Runny magma lets its gas bubble out, so it erupts gently as lava fountains and lava flows: an effusive eruption. Thick, sticky magma traps its gas, so pressure builds until it blasts out ash and rock: an explosive eruption. Magma is thicker when it has more silica and is cooler. The eruptions build the shape: runny lava flows far and makes a wide shield volcano with gentle slopes, while ash and sticky lava pile up near the vent into a steep composite cone.
familyTip: Pour a spoonful of honey and a spoonful of water onto a tilted plate and see which spreads further. Then blow through a straw into a glass of water and into a cup of thick yoghurt: the bubbles escape easily from the water but burst out with a splatter from the thick yoghurt. Look up photos of Mauna Loa and Mount Fuji and spot the difference in shape.

visual.caption: Gentle (effusive) or explosive? Drag each clue, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pour runny and sticky lava, let gas out of three magmas, build a shield and a composite cone, sort six real eruptions, check a park guide.

kid: Magma is melted rock under the ground. Some magma is runny, like warm syrup. Some is thick and sticky, like toothpaste. Magma is thicker when it has more silica in it and when it is cooler.
Magma also holds gas, a bit like a fizzy drink. In runny magma the bubbles rise and escape. Lava fountains up and flows out in rivers. This is a gentle eruption. Scientists call it effusive.
In thick magma the bubbles get stuck. The gas pushes harder and harder. At last it blasts out and shatters the magma into ash and rock. This is an explosive eruption.

The eruptions build the volcano's shape. Runny lava flows a long way before it cools, so it makes a wide volcano with gentle slopes, called a shield. Ash and sticky lava pile up near the vent, so they make a tall, steep cone.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. In England this builds on Year 3 rocks and the Key Stage 2 geography of volcanoes; in the US it meets NGSS 4-ESS2-2 (patterns in Earth's features) and 4-ESS3-2 (reducing the impact of natural hazards). The key words are magma, lava, viscosity (how thick or runny), gas pressure, effusive, explosive, shield volcano and composite volcano (stratovolcano).

Magma viscosity depends mostly on silica and temperature. Basalt magma has about 50% silica and is about 1150 °C, so it is runny. Rhyolite magma has 70% or more and is nearer 750 °C, so it is very sticky. Andesite sits in between. Gas escapes from runny magma, so Hawaiʻi and Iceland mostly see lava flows. In thick magma gas is trapped until it bursts out, as at Mount St Helens in 1980 and Pinatubo in 1991. Shape follows style. Many thin, far-reaching basalt flows build broad shield volcanoes such as Mauna Loa, the largest active volcano on Earth. Layers of ash and thick lava build steep composite cones such as Mount Fuji and Vesuvius.

Common mistakes: thinking every volcano explodes, thinking runny lava builds steep cones, and thinking a low, wide volcano must be small. Children also think sticky magma is hotter, or that lava rivers are the main danger in an explosive eruption. In fact ash and fast, hot clouds of ash and gas are the bigger danger.

In the lab your child pours three lavas and sees how far each spreads. They let gas out of runny, medium and sticky magma, build Mauna Loa and Mount Fuji layer by layer, sort six real eruptions, and catch a park guide's slips.

practice.prompt: A shield volcano grew {a} thin lava layers in each of {b} long eruption periods. How many layers did it grow in all?
practice.hint: Each eruption period adds the same number of thin layers. Multiply.
practice.explain: {a} layers in each of {b} periods is {a} × {b} = {=a*b} layers. Shield volcanoes grow from many thin, runny lava flows stacked up over a very long time.

practice.prompt: Runny lava spread {a} km from the vent. Sticky lava from another vent spread only {b} km. How many km further did the runny lava go?
practice.hint: Subtract the sticky lava's distance from the runny lava's distance.
practice.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} km further. Runny lava flows a long way before it cools, which is why it builds wide, gentle volcanoes.

practice.prompt: Which magma is most likely to erupt explosively?
choices: Thick, sticky magma that traps gas
Runny, hot basalt magma
Magma with no gas in it
practice.hint: Think about whether the gas bubbles can escape.
practice.explain: Thick magma traps gas, so pressure builds until it blasts out. In runny magma the gas escapes gently, and without gas there is nothing to drive an explosion.

practice.prompt: Mauna Loa is very wide with gentle slopes. What was its lava like?
choices: Runny, so it flowed a long way
Sticky, so it piled up near the vent
It had no lava, only ash
practice.hint: Wide and gentle means the lava travelled far before it stopped.
practice.explain: Runny basalt lava flows a long way before it cools. Many such flows built Mauna Loa into a broad shield volcano.

practice.prompt: Why is sticky magma thicker than runny magma?
choices: It has more silica and is cooler
It is hotter than runny magma
It has no gas in it
practice.hint: Two things make magma thick: what is in it and how hot it is.
practice.explain: More silica and a lower temperature make magma thicker. Sticky rhyolite is cooler than runny basalt, not hotter, and all magma holds some gas.

pool.prompt: An ash cloud rose {a} km. A second cloud rose {b} km higher. How high did the second cloud rise?
pool.hint: Add the extra height to the first cloud's height.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} km. Tall ash clouds come from explosive eruptions, where trapped gas shatters thick magma into ash.

pool.prompt: A runny lava flow moved {a} metres each hour for {b} hours. How many metres did it travel?
pool.hint: Same distance every hour, so multiply the distance by the number of hours.
pool.explain: {a} × {b} = {=a*b} metres. Runny lava can keep flowing for hours or days before it cools, so it spreads far from the vent.

pool.prompt: Which shape do layers of ash and sticky lava build?
choices: A tall, steep cone
A wide, gentle shield
A flat plain with no hill
pool.hint: Sticky lava and ash do not travel far from the vent.
pool.explain: Ash and sticky lava pile up close to the vent, so the layers build a steep composite cone, like Mount Fuji.

pool.prompt: Do all volcanoes explode when they erupt?
choices: No: runny magma often erupts gently
Yes, every eruption is an explosion
Only small volcanoes explode
pool.hint: Think of Hawaiʻi and Iceland, where people watch lava rivers.
pool.explain: Runny basalt magma lets its gas escape, so it usually erupts gently as lava flows. Only magma that traps gas explodes.

pool.prompt: In thick magma, what happens to the gas bubbles?
choices: They get trapped, so pressure builds
They escape easily at the top
They turn into lava rivers
pool.hint: Think of blowing bubbles through thick yoghurt.
pool.explain: Bubbles cannot rise through thick magma, so the gas pushes harder until it bursts out in an explosive eruption.

pool.prompt: A volcano is low and very wide. What can you tell?
choices: Its lava was probably runny
It must be a small volcano
It must erupt explosively
pool.hint: Shape tells you about the lava, not the size.
pool.explain: Low and wide means runny lava flowed far. Size is a different question: Mauna Loa is low and wide but is the largest active volcano on Earth.

pool.prompt: What is the biggest danger in an explosive eruption?
choices: Ash and fast, hot clouds of ash and gas
Slow rivers of runny lava
Fountains of lava in one spot
pool.hint: Sticky magma hardly flows. Think about what is blasted out.
pool.explain: Explosive eruptions throw out ash and send fast, hot clouds of ash and gas down the slopes. These are far more dangerous than slow lava.

pool.prompt: What does the word effusive mean for an eruption?
choices: Gentle, with lava pouring out
Violent, with ash blasting out
A volcano that will never erupt
pool.hint: Effusive eruptions happen when gas can escape easily.
pool.explain: An effusive eruption is gentle: lava fountains and flows out because its gas escapes. An explosive eruption blasts out ash.

pool.prompt: Mount St Helens blasted ash about 24 km high in 1980. What was its magma like?
choices: Thick and sticky, trapping gas
Runny, letting gas escape
It had no magma at all
pool.hint: A tall ash cloud means trapped gas burst out.
pool.explain: Mount St Helens has thick, sticky magma. Its trapped gas burst out in an explosive eruption that sent ash about 24 km high.
